summary: A proposed Remote Job Entry protocol for submitting batch jobs from one network host to another. A user connects by Telnet to a special logger for control, and the server then uses FTP to fetch the job input and deliver the output. It was drafted by Chuck Holland and invited comment. It was replaced by RFC 407.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 360 proposes a way to submit a batch job to a remote host. Telnet carries the control commands, while the server arranges for input files and output files to be transferred.

subtitle: A 1972 proposal for submitting remote batch jobs using Telnet and FTP.

tldr.problem: Users needed a way to submit a batch-processing job to another host and receive its output at a remote location.
tldr.mechanism: A user sends control commands over a Telnet connection to an RJE server, which retrieves input files and delivers output files using FTP or a specified host socket.
tldr.outcome: RFC 360 is a proposal for Remote Job Entry and was later obsoleted by RFC 407.

today: RFC 360 is an early Remote Job Entry proposal and was obsoleted by RFC 407. Its control and file-transfer procedures describe the proposal in this document.

sections.title: Submitting a Remote Job
sections.content: Remote Job Entry lets a user at one location cause a batch-processing job to run elsewhere. Under the proposal, the user connects over Telnet to the RJE logger at the server host. The server retrieves the job input, queues it for processing, and sends output files to the requested location.
sections.plainLanguage: A user tells a remote host which batch job to run and where its files are. The remote server retrieves the input and delivers the results.

sections.title: Telnet Control and User Commands
sections.content: The user communicates with the RJE server over a Telnet-like connection to the RJE logger, identified as socket 5 in the proposal. Commands identify the user, specify job input and output paths, request status, or control a job. The RFC says commands and replies are designed for both people and user processes.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet carries the control conversation between the user and the RJE server. Commands identify the user and specify input, output, and job actions.

sections.title: Transferring Job Files
sections.content: The server initiates file transfers under its own control. For many files it uses its local FTP user process to contact an FTP server at the specified host; files may also be sent to a specified host socket. The proposal describes input retrieval, output delivery, output disposition choices, and restart markers for some interrupted transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: The RJE server arranges file transfers, usually through FTP. It can retrieve job input and send output to a host or file destination.

sections.title: Replies and Job Status
sections.content: The server replies to commands with a three-digit code, a blank, and explanatory text. The first digit classifies the reply as information, status, positive acknowledgment, incomplete information, unsuccessful, or incorrect/illegal. Separate reply groups identify topics such as FTP or RJE results.
